text: My name is Samantha Orellana, and I am currently a
postdoc at the Entomology Division of the University of Kansas.
Unfortunately, I couldn't join you in Oslo, but in
name of my colleagues, I will be sharing some updates about
our data mobilization processes using Specify
here at KU.
To give you some context, the KU Entomology Collection
belongs to the University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute and
Natural History Museum.
It's located in Lawrence, Kansas.
As you may know, here is also where the Specify
team and most of the KU collections are located.
However, the Entomology Division is now
in the KU Public Safety building, just a few minutes
away from the main museum.
The KU Entomology Collection, also known as the Snow
Entomological Museum Collection, houses over five
million specimens and hosts a vibrant community of
researchers and students.
In the collection, we use Specify as the main content
management system, and we have digitized about
1.4 million specimens in
approximately two decades.
This represents roughly the 28% of our
holdings. However, this collection
still has the largest insect specimen data set in the
US.
Until recently, only local versions of
Specify were available in the collection, mostly
used by the collection managers and eventual curatorial
assistants.
The last local version used in the collection was
Specify 6,
which was programmed to be decommissioned earlier this year.
So to stay ahead of the change, in 2025,
we plan to migrate to the new Specify 7
online version.
So after updating the mapping for some of the
fields, including the multimedia
fields, the migration process was pretty
straightforward, thanks to the KU Bioinformatics and the
Specify teams.
Now we have access to this online version of our
Specify instance.
Contrary to the local version, the online version allows
access to more users, even outside the collection building,
which has increased the number of students and
researchers using this platform.
Here, we can see the collection object form for data
entry,
which now allows to add new data into
different tables without leaving the form.
For example, if you need to add a new collecting event, you can
do it from the data entry form.
If you need to perform other tasks, for example, a
query, you can also open Specify in multiple
tabs on your browser.
Other advantage compared to Specify 6 is
that the taxon tree can be accessed by multiple users at
the same time.
So instead of finding the tree locked because someone else is
using it, everyone with access can add
and edit names as needed.
Media management was also improved, as we can now add
multiple files directly in the data entry form, where
we can also add controlled vocabulary in the multimedia
metadata fields, including information about
the creator,
which allows us to credit the authors of the
images.
This information can also be edited directly in the attachments
display, which improves the ability to review and improve
data quality.
Both data and images are mapped and packed
into a Darwin Core archive, which is accessible
through an RSS feed with nightly updates.
Through this RSS feed, the data and images are easily
shared and made publicly available in multiple platforms,
such as the Specify online portal.
You can use the QR code to access the portal, which
has all the data and images available from
our Specify instance.
Thanks to the new Specify 7 installation and the
availability of the RSS feed being
constantly updated, we can also update
our GBIF data set constantly, making the
data readily available for research.
Additionally, we can now mobilize the KU Entomology
Collection data directly from Specify to
multiple Symbiota portals, expanding the
information accessibility to different communities of
practice.
These communities include researchers and students
here at the University of Kansas, where we have interns,
undergrads, graduate students, and visitors that
now can not only digitize their specimens
on Specify, but they are also taking advantage of
these new workflows to mobilize the data and
generate additional resources in Symbiota for their
classes or research.
For example, here you can access an
interactive checklist built by one of our students
and also data
and images about type specimens deposited in the KU
collection.
The ability of mobilizing data
more easily using Specify 7 has also been
advantageous to promote international collaborations.
For example, this month, we are starting a new bid
project to mobilize biodiversity information from
Central American species to GBIF.
This
helps us
to share information by following proper biodiversity data
standards and improving the mobilization workflows.
With this, KU will be
able to easily contribute insect data and images from this
region
and increase availability of open biodiversity
information. At the same time, we will be
engaging a global community of biodiversity researchers.
